title: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
summary: Train a cheap student on a teacher's full output distribution: soft targets, temperature, the T-squared loss, sequence and on-policy distillation for LLMs, and when it fails.
outcomes: Explain why a teacher's soft targets carry more training signal than one-hot labels
Compute temperature-softened probabilities and the distillation loss for a small example
Explain why the soft loss is multiplied by T squared and what happens if you forget it
Choose between word-level, sequence-level and on-policy distillation for a language model
Diagnose capacity-gap and fidelity failures and pick a fix such as a teacher assistant

lessons.title: Why a teacher's soft targets beat one-hot labels

blocks.md: Big models and ensembles (several independently trained models whose predictions are averaged) are usually the most accurate thing you can train. They are also the most expensive thing to serve: every request pays for all those parameters. Hinton, Vinyals and Dean (2015) put it with an insect analogy: a larva is built for feeding, the adult for travel, and there is no reason the model you train should be the model you deploy.

**Knowledge distillation** trains a small **student** network to imitate a large, already trained **teacher** (a single big model or an ensemble). The student learns from a **transfer set**, which can be the original training data or extra unlabeled inputs, and its targets come from the teacher's outputs instead of only the human labels. Afterwards you ship the student alone.

The key move is what counts as knowledge. It is tempting to think of a model's knowledge as its weights, which makes it hard to see how a model of a different shape could hold the same thing. The paper's alternative view: the knowledge is the learned **mapping from inputs to outputs**, and a different network can be trained to reproduce that mapping.

nodes.label:
Loss: match soft targets
+ true labels

scenes.caption: Step 1: train the teacher the normal way. It can be huge, heavily regularized, or an ensemble, because nobody has to serve it.
Step 2: freeze the teacher and run it on the transfer set. For every input it emits a whole probability distribution over classes, the soft targets.
Step 3: train the student on the same inputs so its outputs match the soft targets, usually mixed with a small loss on the true labels. Only the student's weights change.
Step 4: deploy the student alone. The teacher's cost was paid once, at training time.

blocks.md: Why should the teacher's outputs be better targets than the labels the teacher itself was trained on? Take an image classifier with five classes: cat, dog, fox, car, truck. The human label for a cat photo is **one-hot**: 1 for cat, 0 for everything else. A trained teacher instead says something like 89.8% cat, 7.4% dog, 2.7% fox, and well under 1% for the vehicles.

blocks.title: One-hot label versus the teacher's distribution (cat photo)

scenes.caption: The one-hot label: all mass on cat. It says nothing about which wrong answers are nearly right and which are absurd.
The teacher's output for the same photo (teacher logits 6, 3.5, 2.5, -1, -2 through a softmax): 89.8% cat, 7.37% dog, 2.71% fox, 0.08% car, 0.03% truck.

The wrong classes are not equally wrong. Dog is about 90 times more likely than car. This ranking of mistakes describes how the teacher generalizes, and it is information the one-hot label throws away.

blocks.md: Hinton et al. give a vivid version: a BMW may have a tiny chance of being mistaken for a garbage truck, but that mistake is still many times more likely than mistaking it for a carrot. Training on the full distribution teaches the student this **similarity structure**. The paper notes two practical consequences: soft targets with high entropy carry much more information per example than a hard label, and their gradients vary less from example to example, so the student can often learn from less data and with a higher learning rate.

blocks.title: Evidence from Hinton et al.: speech acoustic model

scenes.caption: Test frame accuracy of an 85M-parameter speech model (Table 1). Ten models averaged reach 61.1% versus 58.9% for one.
A single model of the same size distilled from the ensemble reaches 60.8%, recovering (60.8 - 58.9) / (61.1 - 58.9), about 86% of the ensemble's gain, at one model's serving cost.

Table 5: trained on only 3% of the data with hard labels, the model overfits and early-stops at 44.5%. With soft targets from a model trained on all the data it reaches 57.0%, close to the full-data 58.9%, without early stopping.

blocks.md: The paper's MNIST experiment tells the same story with error counts. A big regularized net makes 67 test errors; a smaller net trained normally makes 146. The same small net trained to also match the big net's soft targets makes 74, closing most of the gap without seeing any new labeled data.

The teacher's knowledge is its input-to-output mapping, including how much probability it gives to each wrong answer. Distillation transfers that mapping by using the teacher's full output distribution as the training target.

Training the student on the teacher's top-1 prediction alone (pseudo-labeling) is not the same thing. It keeps the teacher's decision but discards the relative probabilities of the other classes, which is exactly the extra signal that makes distillation work.

blocks.question: In Hinton et al.'s speech experiment, a model trained with soft targets on 3% of the data nearly matched one trained on 100% with hard labels. What best explains this?
options: Soft targets contain the correct labels for the other 97% of the data
Each soft target carries information about every class, so one example teaches far more than a one-hot label
Soft targets remove the need for a loss function on the student
The student had more parameters than the teacher
blocks.explain: A one-hot label says only which class is right. A soft target also says how plausible each wrong class is, which encodes what the teacher learned from the full dataset. That extra information per example, plus lower-variance gradients, acts as a strong regularizer, so the small subset goes much further.

blocks.question: A colleague says distillation is pointless if the student has the same architecture as one member of the ensemble teacher, because that architecture was already trained on the data. Based on the speech result, what is the best reply?
options: They are right: the distilled model can never beat a normally trained model of the same size
Only the ensemble matters, so the student should be deleted
The distilled single model recovered most of the ensemble's improvement, so the same architecture trained on soft targets beats the same architecture trained on labels
Distillation only helps when the student is larger than the teacher
blocks.explain: Table 1 of Hinton et al.: same architecture, same data, but trained on ensemble soft targets it reached 60.8% frame accuracy versus 58.9% with hard labels. The training targets, not just the architecture, determine what the network learns.

blocks.md: There is a catch. A good teacher is very confident on most training examples. On MNIST, Hinton et al. describe one image of a 2 getting probability $10^{-6}$ of being a 3 and $10^{-9}$ of being a 7, while another 2 has these reversed. That ratio is exactly the similarity information we want, but probabilities that close to zero barely change a cross-entropy loss, so the student would hardly learn from them.

The fix is a **temperature** $T$ in the softmax. Recall that a softmax turns **logits** (the raw scores $z_i$ before the softmax) into probabilities. Dividing every logit by $T$ before exponentiating gives:

blocks.caption: Hinton et al. Eq. 1. T = 1 is the ordinary softmax; T greater than 1 gives a softer distribution.

blocks.md: Why does this soften the distribution without destroying it? The ratio of two probabilities is $q_i / q_j = \exp((z_i - z_j)/T)$. Dividing by $T$ shrinks every logit gap by the same factor, so the ranking of classes never changes, but large ratios get compressed. For our cat teacher the dog and car logits differ by 4.5, so dog is $e^{4.5} \approx 90$ times more likely than car at $T=1$, but only $e^{4.5/4} \approx 3.08$ times at $T=4$. Now car carries enough mass to matter in the loss.

blocks.title: The same teacher logits at rising temperature

scenes.caption: T = 1: 89.8% on cat. The vehicles get 0.08% and 0.03%, too small to influence training.
T = 2: logit gaps are halved. Cat drops to 66.28%, dog rises to 18.99%, car to 2.0%.
T = 4: a clearly informative distribution (44.22, 23.67, 18.44, 7.68, 5.99). The ranking is unchanged; only the contrast is lower.
T = 8: entropy is 1.545 nats against a maximum of ln 5 = 1.609 for a uniform distribution. The differences are getting small.
T = 20: nearly uniform (24.41% to 16.36%). The information is still there, but only in small deviations from 20% each.

blocks.title: Each class's probability as temperature rises

scenes.caption: The top class: cat falls from 0.90 at T = 1 toward 0.2 (one fifth) as T grows.
The runner-up classes dog and fox first rise, then also flatten toward 0.2. They never cross cat: temperature never reorders classes.
The near-zero classes car and truck rise the most in relative terms. Somewhere around T = 2 to 5 every class carries visible mass while the ranking is still sharp.

blocks.md: In distillation the teacher produces its soft targets at a high temperature, and the student is trained with **the same** temperature in its own softmax so the two distributions are comparable. After training the student runs at $T = 1$ like any other model. The same convention appears in DistilBERT: the temperature is shared by teacher and student during training and set back to 1 at inference.

blocks.prompt: Push T toward infinity. Both teacher and student distributions approach uniform (20% each). Does the distillation signal vanish, or does it turn into something else?
blocks.reveal: It turns into **logit matching**. Hinton et al. show that for $T$ much larger than the logits, and with each example's logits shifted to mean zero, the gradient becomes proportional to $z_i - v_i$, the difference between student and teacher logits. That is exactly the squared-error-on-logits method of Caruana and colleagues, so it is a special case of distillation. Lesson 3 derives it.

blocks.md: Which temperature should you pick? It trades two things. Higher $T$ pays more attention to the very negative logits, which may carry useful knowledge but are also nearly unconstrained by the teacher's own training and therefore noisy. Hinton et al. found that on MNIST, with 300 or more units per layer in the student, all temperatures above 8 gave fairly similar results, but with only 30 units per layer, temperatures of 2.5 to 4 worked significantly better. Small students do best when they can ignore the noisiest part of the teacher. Cho and Hariharan (2019) report that popular choices in prior work are $T \in \{3, 4, 5\}$.

Temperature does not change the argmax. Running the deployed student at T greater than 1 does not change its top-1 predictions at all; it only makes its probabilities less confident. Temperature is a training-time device for distillation (and a separate sampling knob for generative models).
Tune T like any hyperparameter on held-out data. It is not universal: Kim and Rush tested T in 1, 1.5 and 2 for word-level distillation of translation models and found T = 1 worked best.

blocks.question: At T = 1 the teacher thinks dog is 90 times more likely than car (logit gap 4.5). What is that ratio at T = 4?
options: 90, temperature preserves ratios
22.5, the ratio divides by T
About 3.08, because the ratio is exp(4.5 / 4)
1, every class becomes equally likely
blocks.explain: The probability ratio is exp of the logit gap divided by T: exp(4.5 / 4) = exp(1.125), about 3.08. Temperature divides the logit gap, so the probability ratio shrinks exponentially, not linearly. The ordering is preserved; the ratio is not.

blocks.question: You distill a large image classifier into a very small student with 30 units per layer. Following Hinton et al.'s MNIST findings, which temperature range is the best starting point?
options: T = 1, since small students need sharp targets
An intermediate T around 2.5 to 4
T = 20 or more, to transfer every logit
Temperature has no effect on small students
blocks.explain: With 30 units per layer, temperatures of 2.5 to 4 worked significantly better than higher or lower ones. A tiny student cannot absorb all the teacher's knowledge; an intermediate T lets it ignore the very negative, noisy logits while still learning the runner-up structure.

lessons.title: The distillation loss and why it is scaled by T squared

blocks.md: Now the precise recipe. Let $v_i$ be the teacher's logits and $z_i$ the student's. Write $p^{(T)}$ for the teacher's softmax at temperature $T$ and $q^{(T)}$ for the student's. When true labels $y$ are available, Hinton et al. found it best to take a weighted average of two objectives: a soft one that matches the teacher at temperature $T$, and a hard one that is ordinary cross-entropy with the labels at $T = 1$, given considerably lower weight.

blocks.caption: The standard distillation objective. Both terms use the same student logits z; only the temperature differs. Alpha weights the soft term.

blocks.md: KL divergence, $\mathrm{KL}(p \| q) = \sum_i p_i \log(p_i / q_i)$, measures how far a distribution $q$ is from a target $p$. The paper writes the soft term as cross-entropy with the soft targets; using KL divergence instead gives the same gradients. Cross-entropy equals the teacher's entropy plus the KL divergence, $\mathrm{CE}(p, q) = H(p) + \mathrm{KL}(p \| q)$, and $H(p)$ does not depend on the student. For our cat example at $T = 4$: $H(p) = 1.379$, KL $= 0.048$, cross-entropy $= 1.427$. KL is convenient because it is 0 when the student matches perfectly.
The gradient of the soft cross-entropy with respect to a student logit is short and tells you everything:

blocks.caption: Hinton et al. Eq. 2: the student's softened probability minus the teacher's, divided by T.

blocks.md: Two factors shrink this as $T$ grows. One $1/T$ is explicit, from the chain rule through $z_i/T$. The other is hidden in $q_i - p_i$: at high temperature both distributions approach uniform, so their difference shrinks roughly like $1/T$ too. Expanding $\exp(x) \approx 1 + x$ for large $T$ and zero-meaning each example's logits gives Hinton et al.'s Eq. 4:

blocks.caption: N is the number of classes. In the high-temperature limit distillation is logit matching, and the gradient scale falls like 1 over T squared.

blocks.md: That $1/T^2$ is why the soft loss is multiplied by $T^2$. Without it, raising $T$ from 2 to 8 would silently cut the soft term's gradients by up to 16 times relative to the hard-label term (exactly 16 only in the high-temperature limit; in the worked example below the drop is about 9 times, since T = 2 is not yet in that regime), so changing the temperature would also change the effective mixing weight. With the factor, in the paper's words, the relative contributions of hard and soft targets stay roughly unchanged as you vary $T$.

blocks.title: Gradients on the student's logits, worked example

scenes.caption: Soft-target gradient at T = 1, (q - p) / T. Negative means gradient descent raises that logit. The student under-rates cat and dog and over-rates fox.
Compare the hard-label gradient (q - onehot) at T = 1. It pushes dog DOWN (+.041) because dog is wrong. The teacher's soft target pushed dog UP. Labels and teacher disagree about how wrong dog is.
Soft gradient at T = 4 without any scaling: every entry is a few hundredths or less. Raising T has shrunk the signal.
The same gradient multiplied by T squared = 16 (that is, T times (q - p)). Now the vehicles get pushed down hard: at T = 4 the student is told they are over-rated.
T = 20, scaled by 400. It is already close to the logit-matching limit in the next scene.
The limit (z - v) / N after zero-meaning both logit vectors: student-minus-teacher logits divided by 5. Distillation at high T is squared-error logit matching.

blocks.title: Size of the soft gradient as T rises (same example)

scenes.caption: Length of the unscaled gradient vector: 0.1167 at T = 1 down to 0.0016 at T = 20, a drop of about 70 times. The soft term fades away.
Multiplied by T squared the length levels off near 0.6397, approaching the logit-matching limit of 0.6542. Now T controls what is matched, not how loud it is.

blocks.title: Computing the loss for one example
blocks.code:
T, alpha = 4.0, 0.9
v = [6.0, 3.5, 2.5, -1.0, -2.0]  # teacher logits
z = [4.0, 1.0, 2.0, 0.0, -1.0]   # student logits
label = 0                        # true class: cat
p = softmax([a / T for a in v])  # soft targets
q = softmax([a / T for a in z])  # student at T
kl = sum(pi * log(pi / qi) for pi, qi in zip(p, q))
soft = T * T * kl
hard = -log(softmax(z)[label])   # T = 1
loss = alpha * soft + (1 - alpha) * hard

scenes.caption: Setup: temperature 4, soft weight 0.9, the same teacher and student logits as above, true class cat.
Soft targets and the student's softened distribution, both at T = 4.
KL divergence from teacher to student, then the T squared factor (16).
Hard-label cross-entropy at T = 1. The student already gives cat 82.6%, so this term is small.
Weighted sum. The soft term dominates, as Hinton et al. recommend.

blocks.code:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def distill_loss(student_logits, teacher_logits, labels, T=4.0, alpha=0.9):
    # Soft part: KL(teacher_T || student_T), scaled by T*T (Hinton et al.)
    log_q = F.log_softmax(student_logits / T, dim=-1)
    log_p = F.log_softmax(teacher_logits / T, dim=-1)
    soft = F.kl_div(log_q, log_p, log_target=True, reduction="batchmean") * T * T
    # Hard part: ordinary cross-entropy on the true labels at T = 1
    hard = F.cross_entropy(student_logits, labels)
    return alpha * soft + (1 - alpha) * hard

# in the training loop
teacher.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    teacher_logits = teacher(x)   # the teacher is frozen
loss = distill_loss(student(x), teacher_logits, y)
loss.backward()
blocks.caption: PyTorch version. F.kl_div takes the student's log-probabilities first and the target second; batchmean matches the math definition. The official PyTorch tutorial writes the same loss by hand.

blocks.md: Classic bugs: (1) forgetting the T squared factor, so changing T quietly reweights the losses; (2) using `reduction="mean"` in `kl_div`, which divides by batch size times number of classes, not batch size (the [PyTorch docs](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.KLDivLoss.html) warn about this); (3) swapping the arguments; (4) letting gradients flow into the teacher or leaving it in training mode.
Soft gradient = (q - p) / T, which shrinks like 1 over T squared. Multiply the soft loss by T squared so temperature changes what is matched without changing how much it counts.

blocks.question: Your loss uses F.kl_div(log_q, log_p, log_target=True, reduction="mean") on a batch of 32 examples over 1000 classes, then multiplies by T squared. Compared with the intended loss, the soft term is:
options: Correct as written
1000 times too small, because mean divides by every element, not by the batch size
32 times too large
Equal to the cross-entropy instead of KL
blocks.explain: With reduction="mean" PyTorch averages over all 32 x 1000 elements. The KL per example is a sum over classes, so the mathematically correct reduction is batchmean (sum divided by 32). The soft term ends up 1000 times smaller and the hard loss silently dominates.

blocks.question: You raise T from 2 to 8 but your code has no T squared factor. Keeping alpha fixed, what happens to training?
options: Nothing, temperature only affects the soft targets' shape
The student learns the teacher more aggressively
The soft term's gradients shrink by roughly 16 times, so training becomes mostly hard-label training
The hard-label term disappears
blocks.explain: The soft gradient scales roughly as 1 over T squared, and (8/2) squared = 16. Without the compensating factor, the effective weight of the teacher drops sharply and your experiment is really testing a different mixing weight.

lessons.title: Distilling language models: tokens, sequences, on-policy

blocks.md: A language model is a classifier over its vocabulary at every position. So the classic recipe applies token by token: at each position of a training sequence, match the student's next-token distribution to the teacher's. Kim and Rush (2016) call this **word-level distillation**: the loss is the soft cross-entropy summed over positions. It needs the teacher's full probabilities (white-box access) and the same vocabulary for teacher and student.

blocks.title: Word-level targets for the sentence "the cat sat"

scenes.caption: Ordinary training: at each position the target is one-hot on the actual next word.

Word-level distillation: each row becomes the teacher's next-token distribution (illustrative numbers). After the, the teacher says cat 0.61 but dog 0.30, a plausible alternative the one-hot target hides.
The positions still come from a fixed sequence that someone else wrote. That will matter shortly.

blocks.md: Kim and Rush also proposed **sequence-level distillation (Seq-KD)**: run the teacher's beam search (decoding that keeps the few highest-scoring partial outputs at each step) on every training input and train the student with ordinary cross-entropy on the teacher's outputs instead of the human references. This approximates matching the teacher's distribution over whole sequences by its mode. It needs only the teacher's text, not its probabilities, which is the same shape as the common practice of fine-tuning a small model on text written by a larger one. Translation quality below is measured in BLEU, a 0 to 100 score of n-gram overlap with reference translations.

blocks.title: Kim and Rush, English to German, greedy decoding BLEU

scenes.caption: The 84M-parameter 2x500 LSTM student trained on references scores 14.7 BLEU with greedy decoding; the 221M teacher scores 17.7.
Word-level distillation adds 0.7 BLEU (15.4).

Sequence-level distillation adds 4.2 (18.9), beating the teacher's own greedy output. The paper reports the Seq-KD student puts 16.9% of its mass on its greedy output versus 0.9% for the baseline: it models only the teacher's mode.

blocks.md: Both methods share a weakness. During training the student always conditions on prefixes written by someone else (the reference or the teacher). At inference it conditions on **its own** previous tokens, and once it makes a mistake it is in territory it never trained on, so errors compound. Agarwal et al. (2023) call this train-inference distribution mismatch and borrow the fix from imitation learning: train on the student's own outputs.

scenes.caption: Sample a batch of prompts x. With probability lambda the step is on-policy; otherwise it uses a fixed dataset of sequences.
The student generates its own continuation y, mistakes included. No gradient flows through this sampling step.
The teacher scores the student's sequence: at every position it returns its full next-token distribution given the student's prefix.
Minimize a divergence between teacher and student token distributions on those prefixes and update the student. The teacher gives feedback exactly where the student actually goes.

blocks.caption: Generalized KD (Agarwal et al.). D averages a token-level divergence over the sequence; lambda is the fraction of student-generated sequences. Lambda = 0 with forward KL is ordinary supervised KD.

blocks.md: The second design choice is the divergence $D$. Ordinary distillation minimizes **forward KL**, $\mathrm{KL}(p_T \| p_S)$, which heavily penalizes the student for giving low probability anywhere the teacher gives mass: it is **mode-covering**. **Reverse KL**, $\mathrm{KL}(p_S \| p_T)$, penalizes the student for putting mass where the teacher has little: it is **mode-seeking**. When the student is too small to copy the teacher, these give very different students.

blocks.title: Forward vs reverse KL with a student too simple to copy the teacher

scenes.caption: Teacher's next-token distribution after "a cup of": two good answers, tea and coffee at 46% each, four poor ones at 2%.
Simplified toy: the student can only make one smooth bump over this word order. Best fit under forward KL (grid search) spreads out to cover both modes and puts 65% of its mass on the poor words.
Best fit under reverse KL commits to one mode: 92% on tea, 8% on its neighbors, none on coffee. Less diverse, but its samples are almost always good.

blocks.md: MiniLLM (Gu et al., 2023) argues for reverse KL in generative LLMs so the student does not overestimate low-probability regions of the teacher, and optimizes it with on-policy samples. GKD instead uses a generalized Jensen-Shannon divergence $\mathrm{JSD}(\beta)$ that moves between forward-like and reverse-like behavior, and reports the best choice is task-dependent. Hugging Face TRL's GKD trainer exposes these knobs as `lmbda` (student data fraction) and `beta`.

Distillation is now a standard step in building small LLMs. The Gemma 2 report trains its 2B and 9B models with knowledge distillation instead of plain next-token prediction, minimizing the cross-entropy between teacher and student next-token probabilities, on more than 50 times the compute-optimal number of tokens. In an ablation, a 2B model trained on 500B tokens scored 60.3 on average over three benchmarks from scratch versus 67.7 when distilled from a 7B teacher. Its post-training also runs distillation from the teacher on the student's own distribution, citing GKD and MiniLLM.

For language models, decide two things: what sequences you train on (references, teacher outputs, or the student's own samples) and which divergence you minimize (forward KL covers all modes, reverse KL picks one). On-policy training fixes the train-inference mismatch.

blocks.question: A student fine-tuned on teacher-written answers does well on short replies but drifts into nonsense on long ones, while the teacher stays on track. Which change targets the cause most directly?
options: Raise the softmax temperature to 10
Train on the student's own sampled continuations with teacher token-level feedback (on-policy distillation)
Switch from KL divergence to mean squared error on probabilities
Remove the hard-label loss
blocks.explain: The symptom is compounding error from train-inference mismatch: the student never trained on its own imperfect prefixes. On-policy distillation (GKD, MiniLLM) samples from the student and asks the teacher what it should have done at each of those prefixes.

blocks.question: You can call a strong model only through a text API that returns completions, not probabilities. Which method can you still use?
options: Word-level distillation with soft targets
On-policy GKD with forward KL
Sequence-level distillation: train the student with cross-entropy on the teacher's generated outputs
Logit matching at high temperature
blocks.explain: Seq-KD only needs the teacher's output sequences. Word-level KD, logit matching and GKD all need the teacher's token-level probabilities (white-box access) on the relevant prefixes.

lessons.title: When distillation works, when it fails, and what it costs

blocks.md: DistilBERT (Sanh et al., 2019) is a compact case study. The student keeps BERT's architecture but halves the number of layers (removing token-type embeddings and the pooler), because the authors found layer count mattered more for speed than hidden size. Since the hidden sizes match, they **initialize the student from the teacher** by taking one layer out of two. Results are reported on GLUE, a benchmark of nine English language-understanding tasks averaged into a macro-score. It was trained on the same corpus as BERT, on 8 V100 GPUs for about 90 hours.

nodes.label:
L_mlm: masked LM
loss on true tokens

scenes.caption: Initialization: the 6-layer student copies one of every two teacher layers. The ablation says random init costs 3.69 GLUE points.
L_ce: Hinton-style soft-target loss between teacher and student output distributions, same temperature for both.
L_cos: a cosine loss pulls the student's hidden-state vectors toward the teacher's direction. This is feature distillation, transferring intermediate representations, not just outputs.
L_mlm: the usual masked-language-model loss on the real tokens, the hard-label term. The final objective is a linear combination of all three.

blocks.title: DistilBERT ablation: GLUE points lost when removing a piece

scenes.caption: Table 4 of the paper. Dropping the soft-target loss costs 2.96 macro-score points, the hidden-state loss 1.46, the masked-LM loss only 0.31.
Initializing the student randomly instead of from teacher layers costs 3.69 points, the largest single drop. Where the student starts matters as much as what it is trained on.

blocks.md: The result: 40% fewer parameters (66M vs 110M), a GLUE dev macro-score of 77.0 versus BERT-base's 79.5 (about 97% retained), and a CPU inference pass over the GLUE STS-B task at batch size 1 in 410 s versus 668 s, which the paper reports as 60% faster. **Feature distillation** like $L_{cos}$ goes back to FitNets (Romero et al., 2014), which trained a thin, deep student to match a teacher's intermediate layer through an extra learned regressor, needed because the student's hidden layer is smaller.

Now the failures. Intuition says a better teacher makes a better student. Cho and Hariharan (2019) found otherwise: larger, more accurate teachers often do not make better teachers, because a small student cannot mimic them (its KL to the teacher stays high even during training). Their effective fix was to **early-stop the teacher** and to stop distillation partway through training, finishing on the label loss alone, so the student can fit the training loss. They also report that a sequence of distillation steps did not fix the gap in their ImageNet test. Mirzadeh et al. (2019) attack the same **capacity gap** with a **teacher assistant**: an intermediate-sized network distilled from the teacher, which then teaches the student.

blocks.title: Bridging a capacity gap with a teacher assistant

scenes.caption: Direct distillation across a big gap: the student cannot match the teacher's outputs, and Mirzadeh et al. show it can end up worse than with a smaller teacher.
Insert an intermediate network. First distill the teacher into the assistant, a smaller gap it can bridge.

Then distill the assistant into the student. Each step crosses a gap the learner can handle. Cho and Hariharan's alternative: keep one step but early-stop the teacher so its outputs are easier to mimic.

blocks.md: Two more findings sharpen what distillation actually does. Stanton et al. (2021) separate **fidelity** (how closely the student matches the teacher) from **generalization** (how well it does on new data). They find a surprisingly large discrepancy between teacher and student predictions even when the student has enough capacity to match exactly, trace it largely to optimization difficulty, and show that closer matching does not always give better generalization. Furlanello et al. (2018) train **born-again networks**, students the same size as their teachers, which outperformed their teachers on CIFAR and language modeling: the soft targets act as a powerful regularizer, not only as compression.

A more accurate teacher is not automatically a better teacher, and a student that improves is not necessarily copying its teacher. Measure student accuracy directly; try a smaller or early-stopped teacher, or a teacher assistant, when the gap is large.

Costs to plan for:

- **Teacher compute**: every training example needs a teacher forward pass, and on-policy methods also need student generation. Seq-KD front-loads this as a one-time generation job.
- **Storage**: a full next-token distribution over a vocabulary of about 256 thousand entries (Gemma 2's size) is about 1 MB per token position in 32-bit floats, far too much to save for billions of tokens, so you either run the teacher online or keep a truncated approximation.
- **Compatibility**: token-level methods need the teacher's probabilities over the same vocabulary as the student. With only text access you are limited to sequence-level methods.
- **It stacks with other compression**: Kim and Rush pruned their distilled student further, and DistilBERT notes quantization is orthogonal.

Distillation trades extra training compute (running a teacher) for a cheaper model to serve. It works best when the student can realistically imitate the teacher; when the gap is large, shrink it with an assistant or an easier teacher.

blocks.question: You distill a ResNet student from a ResNet-18 teacher and then from a much larger, more accurate teacher. The student does worse with the larger teacher. Which next step is supported by the research in this lesson?
options: Use an even larger teacher so the soft targets are more accurate
Distill through an intermediate teacher assistant, or use an early-stopped teacher
Drop the soft targets and train only on hard labels
Raise T to 100 so the targets become uniform
blocks.explain: This is the capacity-gap failure described by Cho and Hariharan and by Mirzadeh et al. Both an intermediate-size teacher assistant and an early-stopped (less sharp, easier to mimic) teacher are reported fixes. A larger teacher makes the gap worse.

blocks.question: A born-again network (same architecture as its teacher, trained on the teacher's soft targets plus labels) beats its teacher on CIFAR-100. What does this show?
options: The student copied the teacher's weights exactly
Distillation's benefit is not only compression: soft targets also improve generalization
Teachers should always be smaller than students
Distillation only works when fidelity is perfect
blocks.explain: No compression happened, yet the student generalized better. Combined with Stanton et al.'s finding that students often do not match their teachers closely, this shows the soft-target signal acts as a regularizer, not just as a copy mechanism.

blocks.question: You want to distill a model whose tokenizer differs from your student's. Which approach works without extra machinery?
options: Word-level KD, matching probabilities token by token
Logit matching with squared error
Sequence-level KD on the teacher's generated text, re-tokenized by the student
Reverse-KL on-policy distillation
blocks.explain: Token-level losses compare distributions over the same vocabulary at the same positions, which a different tokenizer breaks. Generated text is tokenizer-neutral: the student can tokenize it its own way and train with ordinary cross-entropy.
